about: Corrections to the research facts, applied by tools/compile_facts.py. Each names the fact key, what changes and why; text replacements are asserted against the current notes, so none fails silently. Sources: the verifier checks in research/round1/verify_<topic>.json and this session's own reading.

corrections.why: The fact is an assumption with no source (its own source title says so), but the researcher attached an unrelated Europe PMC search URL to it. Removed the URL so the page does not show a link as if it were a source.

corrections.append_notes: Change to: 'Burton 2018 (Children) is peer-reviewed. Burton 2010 is a Medical Hypotheses paper published before that journal adopted peer review in 2010 (editor-selected): argument plus modelling.' The geometric statement itself is exact for a true scaled copy and needs no empirical source.

corrections.append_notes: Replace 'none found' with: 'No published FFM/H^3 muscularity index for adults was found, but Forbes's model FFM = 10.3 x H^3 (reported by Wang et al. 2012) and Wang's fit FFM = 10.8 x H^2.95 (males aged 5-59, CI 2.83-3.07) are published precedent for FFM proportional to H^3 across growth. Forbes's 10.3 kg/m^3 equals S = 1.8 x 10.3 = 18.5, close to Schutz's adult median FFMI of 18.9.' Status reported. Keep the warning that within adults, FFM scales with about H^2.
corrections.why:
Verifier (index): Wells & Cole 2002 (FFM/HT^2 optimal, FM/HT^6, n = 69, deuterium) and Ramirez-Velez 2018 (n = 4673, fat mass/height^3) check out. The researcher's ABSTRACT-field phrase searches do return 0, as stated.
The search was too narrow, though, and missed a directly relevant paper: Wang Z, Zhang J, Ying Z, Heymsfield SB, 'New insights into scaling of fat-free mass to height across children and adults', Am

set.label: Published fat-free mass over height cubed: no adult muscularity index found, but FFM proportional to H^3 across growth has precedent (Forbes; Wang 2012); within adults FFM scales with about H^2

corrections.append_notes: Use the label 'On average, taller adults have lower girth-to-height ratios (regression powers below 1)'. Status: measured for the regression numbers, but put the structural reading under the disputed key height_exponent_regression_vs_isometry, citing Burton 2010's counter-claim on girths. Note that waist and hip mostly reflect fat.
corrections.why:
Verifier (index): The numbers check out:
- Burton 2012 abstract: 155 men, 162 women, P = 0.00006-0.027.
- Heymsfield 2011 abstract, re-fetched: waist 0.76 +/- 0.08 and hip 0.45 +/- 0.05 in men, adjusted for age and race.
The status and framing overstate them:
(a) These are regression powers. Burton 2010, which the researcher cites, argues that regression underestimates structural exponents. It says girth data 'are

set.label: On average, taller adults have lower girth-to-height ratios (regression powers below 1); whether that is structural is disputed

corrections.append_notes: Label: 'Sport science normalises performance for body size allometrically. Exponents come either from geometric similarity (Jaric's proposal: 0.67 for force) or from fitting to data (Nevill 1992: about 2/3 for VO2max and power).' Add: 'Applied to FFM against adult height, the empirical approach gives about 2 (FFMI); geometric similarity gives 3. These papers cover performance, not body composition.'
corrections.why:
Verifier (index): All three quotes are verbatim: Jaric 2005 'allometric normalization based on theoretical models that presume geometric similarity'; Jaric 2002 b = 0.67 / 1; Nevill 1992 'kg 2/3'.
The characterisation is wrong for Nevill. His 2/3 is 'Based on the fitted power functions', an empirically fitted exponent, and the abstract never mentions geometric similarity. Jaric 2005 is titled 'a proposal for standa

set.label: Sport science normalises performance for body size allometrically: exponents from geometric similarity (Jaric's proposal) or fitted to data (Nevill)

corrections.append_notes: Keep S. Replace 'recommended practice' with 'one proposed approach (Jaric 2005)'. Cite Forbes/Wang 2012 as precedent for FFM proportional to H^3 across growth, and Burton 2007's endorsement of FFM/H^2 within adults as the counterpoint. Draw the landmarks as 'value at 1.80 m'. Present the meatball as a reference shape. Replace 'better' with 'closer to how real men's FFM scales with height (about H^2 to H^2.45)'.

corrections.append_notes: Notes: '12–28% runs from about mean − 1.1 SD to mean + 1.5 SD of Kraemer's DXA strongmen; the lower end was raised to 12% (judgement); the upper end already covers the sumo and heavyweight-powerlifter means (about 26%)'.
corrections.why: Verifier (fat): The stated rationale does not match the numbers. Kraemer's 18.7 ± 1.5 × 6.2 gives 9.4–28.0, so the upper end of 28 is not 'clipped by sumo or powerlifter values (about 26%)'. The lower end of 12 is about −1.1 SD and is the one actually cut. 'S at 12% vs 28% differs by about 18%' is correct (0.72/0.88). Shaw's 17.6% is a self-filmed hydrostatic test relayed by FitnessVolt, a fitness magazine site.
